independent_derivation: Write S=sum_b f(b)^2. Each real square is nonnegative, so S>=0 without using strict positivity. The real nonnegative square root therefore satisfies (sqrt S)^2=S.

The stronger premise S>0 implies sqrt S>0, so the mathematical quotient is defined. Extract its constant squared denominator from the finite sum: sum_b (f(b)/sqrt S)^2=(sum_b f(b)^2)/(sqrt S)^2=S/S=1.

Strict positivity is used to exclude zero denominators and justify S/S=1. The square-root identity itself requires only S>=0, already obtained from the sum of squares. Individual entries may be zero or negative.
expected_rubric_checks: Expands squared quotients and moves the common denominator outside the finite sum.
Uses (sqrt S)^2=S under S>=0 and identifies nonvanishing for cancellation.
Does not replace positive total squared norm by pointwise positive amplitudes or require a circuit as a premise.
edge_case_and_contract_checks: If S=0, every entry is zero. Ordinary normalization is undefined; Lean totalized division would return all zeros and squared sum 0, not 1.
An empty index set has S=0 and cannot meet the premise. A zero-qubit PrimitiveBasis has one element, not zero elements; its nonzero signed scalar normalizes to +1 or -1.
No ancilla, success, circuit efficiency or finite-bit claim follows from this algebraic identity. The separate preparation theorem has an additional nonnegative-amplitude premise.

independent_derivation: For arbitrary nonzero x,y put r=||x||>0, q=||y||>0, e=||x-y||. Algebra gives N(x)-N(y)=(x-y)/r+y(1/r-1/q). Taking norms and using positive r,q gives ||N(x)-N(y)|| <= e/r+q|1/r-1/q|=(e+|q-r|)/r <=2e/r, by the reverse triangle inequality. This computation is valid over R and C because the denominators are positive reals.

In the perturbation statement y is initially arbitrary. Before writing N(y), use ||y|| >= ||x||-||x-y|| >= r-delta>0. Thus y!=0. The reusable inequality gives distance <=2delta/r. Both normalized vectors have norm one, so their distance is also <=2. Combining gives min(2,2delta/r).

If r>=m>0 and 0<=delta<m, then y!=0 and the distance is <=min(2,2delta/m)=2delta/m<2. This is a uniform absolute-error modulus when a positive reference-norm lower bound m is available; y need not itself have norm at least m.

For every t>0 take real two-dimensional x_t=(t,0) and y_t=(t/2,t/2). They are nonzero, ||x_t-y_t||=t/sqrt(2)<t=||x_t||, and the absolute error tends to zero as t tends to zero. Their normalized vectors are (1,0) and (1/sqrt(2),1/sqrt(2)), with constant distance sqrt(2-sqrt(2))>0. Therefore any proposed uniform upper bound g(delta) that depends only on absolute error and tends to zero as delta tends to zero fails on delta_t=t/sqrt(2).

edge_case_and_contract_checks: At delta=0, x=y!=0 and the distance is zero. At delta=r, y=0 is permitted, so the corollary cannot normalize every admitted y. If y is separately known nonzero, the reusable inequality still holds; no false antipodal example under error<=r is needed.
At x=0, N(x) is undefined. In dimension zero the space contains only zero, so the nonzero domain is empty and there is no normalized vector; the stated d>=1 avoids this vacuity.
Distances are between exact representatives. A phase change can contribute to the distance; no minimization over phases, density-matrix distance or fidelity conversion is being invoked.

independent_derivation: J is an isometry, J†J=I, and P=JJ† is the orthogonal projection onto |0^m> tensor H. Put b=Bpsi and eta=(I-P)UJpsi. Since PUJpsi=JJ†UJpsi=JBpsi, the full output is UJpsi=Jb+eta, with J†eta=0 and Peta=0. The two branches are orthogonal. Unitarity and ||psi||=1 give ||Jb||^2+||eta||^2=1, hence ||b||<=1 and ||eta||^2=1-||b||^2.

The operator promise and normalized input give ||alpha b-Apsi||<=epsilon. Reverse triangle implies |alpha||b||-s|<=epsilon, where positivity of alpha is used to take it outside the norm without a sign/phase change. Thus (s-epsilon)/alpha <=||b||<=(s+epsilon)/alpha. Because s>epsilon>=0, Apsi!=0 and b!=0.

Born probability for the specified clean projector is p=||PUJpsi||^2=||b||^2 in (0,1]. Conditioned on success, the joint state is J(b/||b||)=|0^m> tensor (b/||b||), and the normalized system vector is b/||b||. If p<1, the normalized rejected vector is eta/sqrt(1-p), so UJpsi=sqrt(p)J(b/||b||)+sqrt(1-p) eta/sqrt(1-p). If p=1, eta=0 and no normalized rejected state is defined.

Squaring the nonnegative norm inequalities yields ((s-epsilon)/alpha)^2<=p<=((s+epsilon)/alpha)^2; combine the upper bound with p<=1 to obtain the requested minimum. In particular the hypotheses also imply s<=alpha+epsilon, so the positive lower bound is compatible with p<=1.

Apply the supplied normalization result to x=Apsi, y=alpha b and delta=epsilon. Its strict-margin and nonzero premises have now been verified. Positivity of alpha gives N(alpha b)=b/||b|| exactly. Consequently ||b/||b||-Apsi/s||<=2epsilon/s and also <=2 because both vectors are unit. Hence the requested min(2,2epsilon/s) bound.

Let t=alpha||b||. Then |t-s|<=epsilon and t+s<=2s+epsilon. Therefore |p-s^2/alpha^2|=|t^2-s^2|/alpha^2=|t-s|(t+s)/alpha^2<=epsilon(2s+epsilon)/alpha^2. This uses the scaled error ||A-alpha B||<=epsilon; a convention ||A/alpha-B||<=epsilon would have different alpha factors.

The number s^2/alpha^2 is nominal. For example U=I, B=I and A=(alpha+epsilon)I with epsilon>0 satisfy the operator promise with equality and s=alpha+epsilon>epsilon. The actual p is 1 while s^2/alpha^2>1. Approximate containment therefore does not make the nominal quantity a probability.

Clean projection identifies only the P branch. The eta branch generally contains nonzero ancilla/workspace values and remains in the unmeasured output. It cannot be deleted in an unconditioned equality, and cleaning all workspace follows on the successful branch only because the entire workspace is included in K and tested by P.

For independent fresh attempts, T, the attempt of first success, has Pr(T=k)=(1-p)^(k-1)p and Pr(T>k)=(1-p)^k. Summing the geometric tail gives E[T]=1/p. Each attempt uses exactly one input preparation with clean ancillas, one U application and one P test, so each expected operation count is 1/p<=alpha^2/(s-epsilon)^2. Success is almost sure. For p<1 no finite deterministic cap on attempts follows. These are three separately charged operation counts, not gate complexity and not an amplitude-amplification bound.

independent_derivation: Let D=R(a)-R(b). Since R(theta) is real orthogonal and hence unitary over C, R(a)†R(b)=R(b-a). Thus D†D=2I-R(b-a)-R(a-b)=2(1-cos((a-b)/2))I=4 sin^2((a-b)/4) I. For every vector v, ||Dv||=2|sin((a-b)/4)| ||v||, so the induced Euclidean operator norm is exactly 2|sin((a-b)/4)|.

Equivalently, angle-sum identities give the exact signed factorization R(a)-R(b)=2 sin((a-b)/4) R((a+b)/2+pi). The second factor is unitary with norm one. The scalar sign must be retained in the matrix identity even though the norm uses its absolute value.
Using |sin t|<=|t| for every real t yields ||R(a)-R(b)||=2|sin((a-b)/4)|<=|a-b|/2.

For q untouched spectators, their space has dimension k=2^q>=1. In a fixed wire ordering the lifted difference is unitarily equivalent by a common basis permutation to D tensor I_k (or I_k tensor D). Its adjoint product is 4 sin^2((a-b)/4) I_(2k), hence its norm is the same scalar. Alternatively tensor the signed factorization with I_k: the second factor remains unitary. The argument applies to all inputs, including inputs entangled with spectators, and no dimension factor appears because ||I_k||_op=1.
